title: What is known about 1RB0LC_0RC0RB_1LD0RE_0LE1LF_1LA0LB_0LD---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LC_0RC0RB_1LD0RE_0LE1LF_1LA0LB_0LD---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The machine runs a base-5 counter written as markers between blocks; Lean proves its regular sweeps for all block lengths, and an exact fast simulator finds no halt in 1016 steps. It can only halt if two of the rare merges of drifting markers happen close together, which nothing here decides.
Family F05. One of 40 holdouts on the same five-state core; the family's exact block-list map runs this machine for 7.7·1022 steps without a halt.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: One of 40 holdouts on the same five-state core
claims.text: In frame A all 40 machines have states A to E of 1RB0LC_0RC0RB_1LD0RE_0LE?LF_1LA0LB_??--- and differ in D1 (0LF or 1LF), in F0 and in the start state. This machine is that table itself, with D1 = 1LF and F0 = 0LD: step_img proves that every step of the machine is a step of 1RB0LC_0RC0RB_1LD0RE_0LE1LF_1LA0LB_0LD---, and halts_iff that it halts from blank tape if and only if 1RB0LC_0RC0RB_1LD0RE_0LE1LF_1LA0LB_0LD--- halts from blank tape started in state A. The tables of all 40 are compared by frames.py.

claims.title: The family's visit rule and its closed form
claims.text: In frame A a visit starts with the head in state A on the 0 in front of plain blocks (10)^b1 1 (10)^b2 1 … 1 and ends when the head first steps left of that cell. go_spec proves for every depth that a clean visit turns the list l into go n l in exactly goT n l steps (the first block is spread, the rest gets five visits, the first block is folded back 5 shorter); go_closed gives the closed form (b1−5, b2−18, b3−90, …, bk+12·5k−2) when b1 is odd and at least 7, the other blocks even and block i at least 2+18·5i−2. visit states it as a run of this machine. Also proved: the birth of a block, and that the entry into F after a visit that ends in state C on a phase-1 tail reads a 0 (fevent, fevent_reads_zero). The proofs are generated for this machine's own frame-A table; they never use F0.

claims.title: What a clean visit conserves
claims.text: For the blocks after the first, the last one left out: a clean visit (a list the closed form applies to) changes neither the residue of block i modulo 18·5<sup>i−2</sup> nor the drift b<sub>i+1</sub> − 5·b<sub>i</sub> of two neighbours. So these numbers change only at the exceptional events (a block running out, a birth, an entry into F, the left end). This is a law between events, not a proof that the machine never halts.

claims.title: No halt in the first 7.7·10<sup>22</sup> steps (exact block-list map)
claims.text: The machine run as a map on block lists (clean visits by the closed form, a Lean theorem; every other visit by the exact run-length simulator, memoised) reaches step 7.7·1022 without a halt: 58 returns to the left end, 21 entries into F, all reading 0, all with the tape of the proved harmless kind around the head (010001000100[F]011010101010 (15×); 010001000100[F]011010110101 (6×)). The list has 16 blocks at the last left-end event. Its F-events (step and cell read) agree with the plain cell-by-cell simulation of the machine on the first 3·109 steps (4 F-events). This machine's F0 leaves a gadget 0 1 between two blocks after an F-event, so lists with the gadget are simulated on the raw tape, which is slower: hence the smaller step count.

claims.title: Halting would need two exceptional events close together
claims.text: A clean visit cannot halt, and in the runs every exceptional event with long blocks around it ends without a halt; short lists of the same shape do halt. When block i runs out, the next block has about the length of their drift, so a second event close by needs a drift near 0 at that moment. Observed at the left-end events of this run: after step 10<sup>20</sup> the smallest drift in absolute value is 15,542. New drifts are made of sums and differences of earlier blocks, which grow with the run, so close pairs of events should become ever rarer; but nothing proved keeps a drift away from 0, and the figures are sampled at the left-end events only.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 81,916 cells have been visited and 31,046 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.618).

claims.title: The sweeps, for all block lengths
claims.text: Fifteen pieces of a sweep (the leftward wave across a block and across a carried marker, the turns at a marker in each phase, the rightward waves, the overflow at the left end) and nine whole sweeps: one per phase of the last marker, with one and two carries, and overflows with one and two markers.

claims.title: An exact fast simulator
claims.text: The run-length simulator c/rl.c of the family lead (shift rules found and applied automatically, like symtm on concrete numbers) gives the same tape at every sweep end of the first 108 steps as the run without shift rules and as the plain simulator.

claims.title: The counter rules
claims.text: To 10<sup>11</sup> steps, 253,714 of the 253,757 sweeps are regular turns and 13 are overflows, each exactly as the two rules say; the other 30 are merges.

claims.title: No halt in 10<sup>16</sup> steps
claims.text: The fast simulator runs 10,000,000,174,322,299 steps without a halt; F is entered 15 times and reads a 0 every time.

claims.title: Merges of separated markers never halt
claims.text: All 48 merges of two markers with at least 12 words of block on either side (each failing turn, each phase of the marker before it, with and without a carried marker after it) run symbolically, for all block lengths, for 12 sweeps or until the carry leaves them: none halts.

claims.title: Same class (same tapes or same markers, not the same run) as 1RB0LC_0RC1RF_1RD0RE_1LE0RA_0LA0LE_0RB---
claims.text: Class V of the five runs of the family. The mirrored members have the same markers at every sweep end from sweep 159,760 on.

claims.title: Halting needs two merges close together
claims.text: 39 of 2,000 random short tapes of the same shape halt within 20,000 steps, while separated merges never halt. Whether the drifting counter ever brings two merges together is a question about its arithmetic that nothing here settles.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Only if two merges ever meet; a question about the long-run arithmetic of the counter.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB0LC_0RC1RF_1RD0RE_1LE0RA_0LA0LE_0RB--- up to renaming and mirroring, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each. explainer.lede: Nobody knows. The machine counts in base 5 with markers that drift along the tape and now and then collide; a collision has never halted it, and it could only halt if two collisions came close together.

facts.text: proved in Lean for all block lengths.
No halt in the C simulator; 81,916 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.

sections.heading: One core, forty machines
html:
This machine is one of 40 holdouts built on the same five states. Written in one common frame (frame A), every one of them has the table

stateABCDEF
reads 01RB0RC1LD0LE1LAF0
reads 10LC0RB0RE0LF or 1LF0LBhalt

and they differ in three things only: the bit that D writes on its way into F (D1), what F does on a 0 (F0), and the state the run starts in. This machine is the core itself (frame A) with D1 = 1LF and F0 = 0LD, started in state A. Lean proves this for the machine's own table (halts_iff in lean/Family.lean): it halts from blank tape exactly if the frame-A table halts from blank tape in state A.

What the 40 machines share. States A to E never enter F while they run the nested counter, so between two entries into F all 40 machines do the same thing, and one law covers them. In frame A the tape is a list of blocks (10)^b; a visit to the list [b1, …, bk] makes five visits to the list without its first block. When the blocks are large and of the right parity (a clean visit) this has a closed form: b1 loses 5, block i loses 18·5i−2, the last block gains 12·5k−2. Both the recursion and the closed form are Lean theorems for every depth, on each of the 40 tables (go_spec, go_closed). Two quantities are therefore conserved by every clean visit (visit_conserves): the residue of block i modulo 18·5i−2, and the drift bi+1 − 5·bi of two neighbouring blocks (neither the first nor the last). The residue fixes at which phase and with which small value a block will run out; the drift is the length the next block still has at that moment.

This machine's run, seen from the left end. Each time the head comes back to the left end of the tape (frame A) the tape is a plain list of blocks. Move the slider through these moments: the middle blocks drain at their fixed rates, the last block grows, a block that runs out disappears and its neighbours merge, and new blocks are born at the right end. The list is from the exact block-list map (below), which was checked against the plain simulation of the machine on the F-events of the first 3·109 steps.

How far it has been run. The exact block-list map (clean visits by the proved closed form, every other visit by an exact run-length simulation, here on the raw tape where the F-event leaves a gadget 0 1 between two blocks) runs this machine for 7.7·1022 steps without a halt: 58 returns to the left end, 21 entries into F, every one reading 0, with the tape around the head 010001000100[F]011010101010 (15×, F reads 0); 010001000100[F]011010110101 (6×, F reads 0). Every one of these entries is the kind proved harmless in Lean (fevent, fevent_reads_zero): a visit ends in state C on the 0 of a phase-1 tail, and F then reads the last cell of a 1000.

The sixteen variants. The 40 machines are 16 choices of (D1, F0), each from up to three start states. Machines marked with the same run letter had exactly the same block list at their last left-end event (an observation, not a proof); they are still separate halting questions until that is proved.

Why this does not settle halting. A clean visit cannot halt, and an isolated exceptional event (one block running out between long neighbours, a birth, the harmless F-event) does not halt in any run so far. Short block lists of the same shape do halt, so a proof has to control the block lengths: it would have to show that two exceptional events never fall close together, that is, that a drift is never small when its block runs out. The drifts only change at exceptional events, where they are sums and differences of large earlier blocks; nothing is known that keeps them away from 0. Observed in this run, at the left-end events: after step 1020 the smallest drift in absolute value is 15,542. That is evidence, not a proof, and it is sampled at the left-end events only.

sections.heading: A base-5 counter of markers
html: Stop the machine each time the head steps onto a new cell at the growing end. The tape is then always
1 (0010)b0 m1 (0010)b1 … mk (0010)bk 000
long blocks of the word 0010 separated by markers, each in one of six phases: 1 (0), 0 (0′), 0011 (1), 011 (2), 11 (3), 00111 (4).

Between two such moments the head makes one sweep: a wave runs from the end toward the start, passing every marker in phase 4, and turns at the first marker that is not; that marker goes up one phase, and on the way back the phase-4 markers are reset to phase 0. The phases are the digits of a counter in base 5 that counts the sweeps. When every marker is in phase 4 the wave runs to the start of the tape and the counter gains a digit (a new marker at the end).

The blocks around a marker change with its phase (phase 0 takes two words from the block before it, phases 0′ and 3 one), so the markers drift toward the start, the last one fastest. When a marker has used up the block before it, it merges with the marker there: a few special sweeps, after which the counter goes on. Lean proves the regular sweeps for all block lengths.

Run the counter. The tape between two sweeps, written as its first block b0 and the markers with the block after each. Each step is one sweep of the machine by the two regular rules; the run stops at a merge, where a marker has used up the block before it and the machine does something special.

sections.heading: Where it could halt
html:
The only halting transition is F1, and F is entered only at some merges (and, in two of the sixteen machines, on a detour that does what the others do in one step). Every entry into F so far has read a 0. Every merge of two markers with long blocks around them runs, symbolically and for all block lengths, without halting. But short tapes of the same shape, where two short blocks meet, often halt.

So the machine halts only if two merges ever happen close together on the tape. The counter is deterministic, and the block lengths it makes look very regular (many are close to multiples of powers of 5), but nothing here decides whether such a coincidence ever comes.
Sixteen holdouts run this counter, in five distinct runs; this machine is in class V. The family is described in full on the page of 1RB0LC_0RC0RB_1LD0RE_0LE0LF_1LA0LB_0LC---.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.618).
After 109 steps the tape spans 81,916 cells (53 left of the start, 67,298 right), with a density of 1s of 0.379.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machines below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in any of the others, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: Marker counter (class V): a base-5 counter of markers between 0010-blocks, whose markers drift and merge; halting needs two merges close together. No halt in 10^16 steps.
